# Introduction

Physical inactivity is one of the leading modifiable risk factors for
non-communicable disease [@bauman2012]. Despite consistent public health
messaging, a large share of the adult population does not meet current activity
recommendations [@garber2011].

## Aim of the thesis

This thesis examines whether a supervised 12-week training programme improves
cardiorespiratory fitness in older adults, and whether the response differs by
baseline fitness.

## Research questions

1. Does supervised training increase peak oxygen uptake relative to usual care?
2. Is the training response modified by baseline fitness?
3. Are changes in fitness accompanied by changes in cardiometabolic markers?

## Structure of the thesis

@sec-background reviews the literature. @sec-methods describes the design and
the statistical approach. Results follow in @sec-results, and @sec-discussion
places them in context.
